Formal Verification of a One-Master One-Slave SystemC/TLM AMBA AHB Model with UPPAAL Timed Automata

C. Deepthi Sree (BL.EN.U4ECE23107), G. Sohan (BL.EN.U4ECE23117), K. Lochana Reddy (BL.EN.U4ECE23127)
Department of Electronics and Communication Engineering, Amrita Vishwa Vidyapeetham
23ECE337 System on Chip — Simulation and Analysis-based Assignment, Batch B, Semester VII

Abstract—We repeat, for the one-master one-slave (1M1S) configuration, the model-checking experiment of Pockrandt, Herber and Glesner on a SystemC/TLM 2.0 model of the AMBA AHB bus [1]. Starting from the UPPAAL timed-automata model of the design, we check the three properties of the paper's Table II that apply to 1M1S: deadlock freedom, eventual bus grant to master 1, and a bound on communication time after a grant. For the timing property we add one clock to the model, as the paper describes, and search for the smallest bound that holds. We also recreate the missing counter reset reported in the paper and check how it shows up in our model. Every number in Section IV is produced by a script from saved UPPAAL output.

Index Terms—AMBA AHB, SystemC, transaction-level modeling, timed automata, UPPAAL, model checking.

I. Introduction

Transaction-level models (TLM) in SystemC let designers simulate a system on chip long before RTL exists, but a simulation run follows only one ordering of concurrent processes. Corner cases in bus protocols, such as a counter that is not reset after a split transaction, can therefore survive many simulation runs. Model checking explores every reachable state of a formal model instead.

Reference [1] transforms SystemC/TLM designs into UPPAAL timed automata [3], [4] and applies the method to an industrial TLM 2.0 model of the AMBA AHB [5]. Our assignment repeats that experiment for the smallest configuration, one master and one slave (1M1S), and compares our measurements with the 1M1S column of the paper's Table II.

II. Reference Work

The key contribution of [1] is an optimised encoding of the TLM 2.0 payload event queue (PEQ). Instead of a global clock array and a sorted queue, each pending notification is held by its own automaton with a local clock c (paper Fig. 4), and a second automaton invokes the callback (paper Fig. 5). This reduces the number of clocks and makes symmetry easier to exploit.

The AHB case study has a tlm2_master that issues read and write bursts by blocking transport to a master_to_ahb adapter, which splits them into AHB transfers over the bus to ahb_mem slaves. The paper checks four properties for 1M1S up to 2M2S. For 1M1S it reports 74,345 states, with 0:07 for deadlock freedom, 0:05 for bus grant to M1 and 0:17 for communication in time. It also reports a bug found during verification: a counter that stores the number of completed transfers before a transaction is split was not reset, so all split transactions after the first one failed (Section VI-B of [1]).

III. Model and Method

A. The 1M1S model

Our model amba_AHB_1M1S.uppaal.xml contains 66 automata instances built from 44 templates: the SystemC scheduler and initialiser, the clock clk (period 20 time units), the traffic generator TLM2_M1, the adapter AHB_M1, the bus AHB_Bus and the memory AHB_S1. We could not regenerate it with the STATE tool, so it was reduced by hand from the 2M2S model: the master-2, slave-2 and second traffic-generator instances were removed, number_of_slaves in the traffic generator was changed from 2 to 1, and the initial readyprocs count from 3 to 2. The bus templates are unchanged and still loop over two masters and two slaves; the unused master-2 and slave-2 ports are bound to channels that no automaton uses. In each round the traffic generator writes and then reads a 3-beat burst at address 0, waits (wait_clks = 20) and starts again, so the model runs forever.

B. PEQ encoding in our model

Each PEQ is built from three templates: peq_notify accepts a notification and hands it to a free element, four peq_element instances each hold one notification with a local clock c and the invariant c <= delay (the automaton of paper Fig. 4, Fig. 2 here), and peq_fetch calls the callback and signals deactivate (paper Fig. 5, Fig. 3 here). The model has no global PEQ clock array, so it uses the optimised encoding of [1].

C. Properties

Deadlock freedom is checked as A[] not deadlock. For bus grant we use the leads-to property AHB_M1$m_bus_req_pending --> AHB_M1$m_bus_granted: whenever the adapter has a pending bus request it is eventually granted. A reachability query E<> would only show that one such run exists, so we report it separately. The properties that involve master 2 do not apply to 1M1S.

D. Timing instrumentation

For communication in time, [1] adds an extra clock x that is reset whenever a master is granted the bus. We generate amba_AHB_1M1S_timed.uppaal.xml from the unchanged model with a script that adds a global clock x and a flag M1_isCommunicating. Both edges where the adapter records a grant set x = 0 and the flag to true; both edges where b_transport finishes a transaction set the flag to false. The new variables are never read by the model, so its behaviour is unchanged, although the extra clock enlarges the state space. We then search for the smallest N for which A[] M1_isCommunicating imply x <= N holds, by doubling from one clock period and then bisecting.

E. Bug study

The adapter resets m_txn_count = 0 when a write or read transaction is cleaned up (tlm2_master_to_ahb.cpp lines 120 and 154 of the STATE-2.1 amba_AHB example, included in systemc_source/; the UPPAAL model merges each clean-up into one update annotated with lines 116 and 150). A second derived model removes both resets. We check deadlock freedom and the liveness property M1_isCommunicating --> !M1_isCommunicating (every started transfer finishes) on both versions.

V. Discussion and Limitations

  • Our state counts and times differ from the paper's. We report both and have not tried to tune the model or the search options to match.
  • The 1M1S model was reduced by hand, not regenerated from SystemC. The SystemC sources of the STATE-2.1 examples/amba_AHB design (bus, memory slave, master adapter, traffic generator and defines.h) are included in systemc_source/. defines.h describes the original 2M2S design (MASTER_N = 2, SLAVE_N = 2); only the traffic generator's number_of_slaves was reduced to 1.
  • The communication-in-time bound depends on where we start and stop measuring. We start at each grant, as [1] does, and stop when b_transport finishes the transaction. Because x restarts at every grant, N bounds the time from the most recent grant to the end of the transaction, not the length of the whole transaction. Measuring from the first grant of a transaction would need a second clock and is left for future work.
  • UPPAAL 4.1.26-1, which we used first, stopped running because its start-up check failed (it printed an HTTP 301 page). All results here come from the version listed in Section IV-A.

VI. Conclusion

We repeated the 1M1S part of the AMBA AHB experiment of [1] with UPPAAL. {{CONCLUSION_SENTENCE}} The bug study shows how the missing counter reset appears in our model. Extending the work to 2M2S would need the full model and far more memory, which is why we limited this assignment to 1M1S.
